passage:
Subject: Your lab notes, and a confession

Trisha,

Congratulations on topping the structures test again. Honestly, when the list went up my stomach dropped, and I sulked in the canteen for about an hour. Then I remembered you had asked for my beam-deflection notes on Friday. For a moment I thought about "forgetting" to send them. They are attached now, with the diagrams. Since first year, your marks have made me start revision two weeks earlier than I ever used to, and my own scores have climbed because of it. I still plan to beat you in the final semester 🙂 so keep working.

Ojas

qa.q: Which test did Trisha top again?
qa.a: Trisha topped the structures test again.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when the list went up, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Ojas felt hurt and competitive; the stomach dropped and the sulking in the canteen for about an hour show it.

qa.q: What could Ojas do to keep this rivalry useful in the final semester?
qa.a: Ojas could keep starting revision early and keep sharing notes, treating Trisha's marks as a standard to reach rather than something to block.

qa.q: How might Trisha read this email?
qa.a: Trisha may find it honest and generous, since Ojas admitted the sulking yet still sent the notes that were asked for. 🙂

grounding: A classmate rival pushes the writer's standard while the writer stays decent by sending the notes.

passage: Imran caught Usha at the bus stand in the kasba and lowered his voice. "They're saying at the tea stall that you were sacked from the stationery shop for keeping extra change." Usha's ears burned, and her first thought was to march over and shout it down. Instead she breathed, took the ledger she kept herself, and walked to the shop owner. She said calmly that she had heard the story and wanted him to see her accounts. That evening she told her mother the same, plainly. After that she did not chase each whisper at the well or answer the giggling girls. She opened the shop at nine, as always. By fair week the owner had told two customers, unasked, that her counter never ran short. Imran still noticed her jaw tighten whenever the tea stall came up.

qa.q: Where did Imran tell Usha about the story?
qa.a: Imran told Usha at the bus stand in the kasba.

qa.q: What was Usha's first urge when she heard the story, and what does it suggest?
qa.a: Her first thought was to march over and shout it down, and her burning ears suggest anger and embarrassment.

qa.q: What could Usha do if the whispers keep coming?
qa.a: She could keep opening the shop at nine, keep her accounts open to the people who matter, and keep speaking calmly instead of chasing each whisper. 🙂

qa.q: How might the shop owner see Usha's visit with the ledger?
qa.a: The owner may see someone with nothing to hide who values his trust, which fits how he later told customers her counter never ran short.

grounding: False stories about Usha spread and she addresses key people calmly, ignores the whispers and lets her work speak.

passage:
Late evening. Sunaina, new in Pune, texts her brother Vikas.

Vikas: How's the new city? Made friends yet?
Sunaina: Not really. Evenings are the worst. I sit in my PG room scrolling everyone's photos from home 😔
Vikas: That will make it worse, na.
Sunaina: I know. Today I walked at six instead. Same lane, same chai stall. The stall uncle nodded at me.
Vikas: That counts!
Sunaina: Joined the Saturday badminton group nearby too. Knew nobody, played badly, went anyway.
Vikas: And?
Sunaina: Still lonely. But a girl called Meera said come again next week. Papa says it took him months in Bhopal in his first job. I'm giving it till winter 🙂
Vikas: Send me a photo of your racket 🏸

qa.q: What group did Sunaina join near her PG?
qa.a: Sunaina joined the Saturday badminton group nearby.

qa.q: What does Sunaina's message about the evenings suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she felt lonely and low, since she said evenings are the worst and she sat in her PG room scrolling photos from home.

qa.q: What would you advise Sunaina if the loneliness lasts through the first months?
qa.a: Keep the small routines, the six o'clock walk and the badminton, and remember what Papa said about it taking months. 🙂

qa.q: How might Vikas feel while reading these messages?
qa.a: Vikas seems concerned for his sister but encouraged, since he warned her off scrolling and then cheered at her walk and badminton.

grounding: Sunaina is lonely in a new city and builds routines and joins a group while accepting it will take months.

passage: I'm Suraj, and I share a hostel room with Naveen. Every Sunday evening he calls his mother, and I hear him slip into Malayalam, faster and louder than his English ever is. After the call he goes quiet and stares at the train calendar over his bed, with the December date circled in red. But something changed after Onam. He bought a second-hand steamer, and now on Thursdays he makes puttu in the common kitchen for whoever is on our floor. Three or four of us show up. Last week he taught the boy from Assam to say "nalla ruchi", which means tasty. I can't say what goes on inside him; when I asked, he laughed and said the mess sambar is just wrong. But the calendar isn't the only thing on his wall now. There's a rota for Thursday cooking too.

qa.q: What does Naveen make on Thursdays for his floor?
qa.a: He makes puttu in the common kitchen, using a second-hand steamer.

qa.q: What might Naveen be feeling when he goes quiet after the Sunday call?
qa.a: He seems to miss his mother and home, though Suraj admits he cannot say what goes on inside Naveen.

qa.q: How do the Sunday calls and the Thursday cooking work together for Naveen?
qa.a: The calls keep him close to home, while the cooking builds a small anchor on his floor so he is not living only for December.

qa.q: How does Suraj seem to see Naveen's homesickness?
qa.a: Suraj sees it kindly but with uncertainty; he happily turns up for the puttu yet says he cannot know for sure what Naveen feels. 🙂

grounding: Naveen misses family food and language, calls home and also builds small anchors in the hostel.

passage: Ishita here, from flat 4A. When Aditi moved into 4B, I barely noticed. Then she kept "happening" to be at the lift at eight. First there was only a nod. Next she asked where the laundry was. A few days later she carried my parcel up from the gate and set it at my door, hovering a second too long before a small smile. She looked nervous each time, but she kept coming back. On Friday she asked if I wanted to share an auto to the market, and I said yes. Honestly, I would never have knocked on her door myself; I'd have waited for the awkwardness to pass. I can't be sure what she felt, maybe she was only being polite, but now we have a market plan for Sunday.

qa.q: What did Aditi carry up for Ishita?
qa.a: Aditi carried Ishita's parcel up from the gate.

qa.q: What might Aditi have been feeling as she hovered at Ishita's door?
qa.a: Aditi was probably nervous and hopeful, since Ishita noticed the hovering and the small smile, though Ishita admits she cannot be sure.

qa.q: What could Aditi try next after the shared auto ride?
qa.a: Aditi could keep the small, repeated contact going, such as a chat at the lift or an invitation for tea, so the friendship keeps growing.

qa.q: Why might Ishita not have started the friendship herself?
qa.a: Ishita says she would never have knocked, so she may also fear awkwardness, and Aditi's small steps made it easy to say yes.

grounding: Aditi reaches out to a neighbour through small repeated contact instead of waiting to be invited.

subtype: Landlord or neighbour × Feeling unsafe or cheated [Receiver]
passage: The student welfare desk was empty except for Nandini, a final-year volunteer, when Farida walked in turning a folded paper over in her hands. "My landlord says the deposit is settled and the extra maintenance is just verbal," she said. "He gets annoyed when I ask for anything on paper." Since arriving from Lucknow in July she had told her parents nothing; they had stretched to pay her fees and she did not want them to worry. Nandini listened, then said she had felt the same fear in her first year. She helped Farida write down what had been agreed, suggested asking the landlord to sign it, and wrote the welfare officer's extension on the back. "Keep two numbers of people you trust," she said. "And tell your parents tonight, before it grows." Farida's shoulders dropped for the first time that afternoon.

qa.q: Where had Farida arrived from in July?
qa.a: Farida had arrived from Lucknow.

qa.q: What was Farida worried about, and why had she told her parents nothing?
qa.a: She was worried about the unclear deposit and maintenance, and she kept it from her parents because they had stretched to pay her fees and she did not want them to worry.

qa.q: What steps did Nandini suggest to Farida?
qa.a: Nandini suggested writing down what was agreed and asking the landlord to sign it, keeping two numbers of trusted people, calling the welfare officer, and telling her parents that night.

qa.q: How might the landlord see Farida's request for something on paper?
qa.a: He seems to see it as distrust or hassle, since he gets annoyed, though a signed note would protect both sides.

grounding: A newcomer feels vulnerable with a landlord's verbal promises and is guided to get things in writing, keep trusted contacts and tell family.

passage: I'm Pankaj. When I moved to Bengaluru for my first job, my gaming squad became my whole evening. Six hours some nights. I told myself I couldn't be lonely with voices in my headset. Three months in, I noticed I hadn't spoken aloud to anyone since Monday. I didn't want to give up the squad; they were the ones who had asked how my interview went and celebrated when I got the job. Then Uma, who plays with us, mentioned she lived in Indiranagar too. We met for filter coffee and were awkward for ten minutes, then not. I still play most nights, but Saturday mornings I now walk with Uma and two of her friends. The squad knows, and they cheer me on. Looking back, I needed both kinds of company.

qa.q: Which city did Pankaj move to for a first job?
qa.a: Pankaj moved to Bengaluru.

qa.q: Why was Pankaj reluctant to give up the squad, and what does that show?
qa.a: The squad had asked how the interview went and celebrated the job, so Pankaj felt cared for and valued them.

qa.q: What is a balanced way for Pankaj to spend evenings and weekends?
qa.a: Pankaj can keep playing with the squad most nights and keep the Saturday walks with Uma and her friends, so online and in-person company sit side by side.

qa.q: How might Uma see meeting Pankaj for filter coffee?
qa.a: Uma may see it as a natural step from friendly voices to a real friend, since Uma mentioned living in Indiranagar too and later walks with Pankaj on Saturdays.

grounding: Pankaj relies on online friends yet values them while also building in-person connection.

passage: The hostel emptied out the night before Diwali, trolley bags rattling down the corridor. Sachin's ticket home had waitlisted, and rebooking cost more than he had. His mother called on video while a noisy crowd of leavers passed behind him. "Sab theek hai, ma, everyone's here, big dinner," he said, and hung up smiling. Then he sat in the empty mess, sure that every other person in the building had a crowd. Chandrika from the third floor came in to make instant noodles. She had stayed too. "You look like I felt last week," she said. "Honestly? I've eaten alone since September." Sachin's throat tightened. "Me too," he said at last, and the words felt lighter than the smile he had put on for the call.

qa.q: Why did Sachin stay in the hostel over Diwali?
qa.a: His ticket home had waitlisted and rebooking cost more than he had.

qa.q: Why did Sachin tell his mother that everyone was there for a big dinner?
qa.a: He seems ashamed of being alone and wanted to look fine, and the smile as he hung up suggests he was hiding how he really felt.

qa.q: What might Sachin do after Chandrika's honest words?
qa.a: Sachin could keep talking with Chandrika, perhaps share meals with her, and tell his mother the truth when he is ready.

qa.q: What is it like for Chandrika to say she has eaten alone since September?
qa.a: It may feel like a risk and a relief, because saying it lets Sachin see that he is not the only one.

grounding: Sachin believes everyone else has friends, pretends to be fine to his mother, then has one honest conversation.

passage:
Monday. Simran leaned over the partition. "We're going to the dosa place at one. Come?" Maria's cheeks warmed. She had a half-finished deck and a heavy head from a poor night. "Maybe next time," she said, and ate a sandwich at her desk.

Thursday. Simran asked again, lighter this time. Maria felt the same pull to say no and said it, then heard the group laughing by the lift and felt the office go quiet.

The following Tuesday. Simran did not ask; she just picked up her bag. "Coming?" Maria's tiredness had not gone anywhere, but she closed her laptop. Over dosas she learned Simran had also moved to the city alone, two years ago. She laughed at a story about the boss's umbrella. On the way back Simran said, "Same time Thursday?"

qa.q: Where did the group go for lunch?
qa.a: The group went to the dosa place.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling when she said "Maybe next time"?
qa.a: She felt shy and tired, with a half-finished deck and a heavy head from a poor night.

qa.q: What small step helped Maria on Tuesday?
qa.a: She said yes even though her tiredness had not gone anywhere, and she closed her laptop and went along.

qa.q: How might Simran have seen Maria's earlier refusals?
qa.a: Simran kept asking lightly and had moved to the city alone too, so Simran may have understood the hesitation rather than taking it as rejection.

grounding: A colleague invites Maria to lunch; after declining twice from shyness and tiredness she says yes and a friendship starts.

passage:
Late at night, Minakshi texts her cousin Bhavna.

Minakshi: you awake?
Bhavna: yes, what's up?
Minakshi: Not sure. Since the semester started in this new city I've barely left my room except for classes.
Minakshi: I sleep at 4, wake at noon and feel worse. I can't be bothered to eat properly.
Bhavna: That sounds heavy. Since when?
Minakshi: Three weeks maybe? I keep thinking there's no point telling anyone, nothing will change.
Bhavna: I get why it feels like that. But you told me just now, and I'm glad. Can we try one thing?
Minakshi: what
Bhavna: The campus counsellor. I'll stay on the phone while you fill in the form, and tomorrow you call Mummy.
Minakshi: ...okay. I'll send it tonight. Please stay till it's done.
Bhavna: I'm here.

qa.q: How long has Minakshi felt this way?
qa.a: Minakshi says about three weeks, maybe.

qa.q: What is Minakshi worried about when she says nothing will change?
qa.a: Minakshi thinks there is no point telling anyone, fearing that reaching out will not help.

qa.q: What did Bhavna suggest, and why might it help?
qa.a: Bhavna suggested the campus counsellor and calling Mummy, which could bring support from people trained and people who care while Bhavna stays on the phone. 🤍

qa.q: What is it like for Bhavna to receive this message late at night?
qa.a: Bhavna seems concerned but steady, saying it sounds heavy, that Bhavna is glad Minakshi said it, and offering to stay until the form is done.

grounding: Weeks of isolation drain Minakshi's energy and sleep; she notices it and reaches out to a cousin, then a campus counsellor.
